planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Cupido stays low and wide rather than climbing upward, so give it room to spread rather than height.

directions: Cupido is a Dutch-raised dwarf sport of Japanese andromeda selected for a flattened, mounding habit far lower and wider than the species, making it useful as a shaded groundcover or low edging where a taller pieris would be out of scale. Small clusters of white, urn-shaped flowers appear in spring against glossy dark-green leaves that flush a soft bronze-red on new growth. Because the habit stays so low, mulch generously to keep the shallow, spreading root zone consistently moist without smothering the crown. Site it out of harsh winter wind and direct afternoon sun to prevent leaf scorch on its compact foliage.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Crispa's undulating leaf margins show best when the plant is viewed at close range along a path or entry.

directions: Crispa is an old European selection of Japanese andromeda grown chiefly for foliage texture rather than flower color, its glossy leaves rippling and twisting along the margins instead of lying flat like the species. Drooping clusters of small white flowers open in spring, but the crinkled leaf surface remains the main draw through every season of the year. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil that all pieris require, since dry or alkaline conditions quickly show up as leaf yellowing on a plant chosen for foliage interest. Shelter from harsh winter sun and wind protects the textured leaves from the marginal scorch that mars flatter-leaved cultivars less noticeably.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Curly Locks Pieris (Contorted Twisted-Stem Dwarf Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Curly Locks grows very slowly, so treat it as a specimen accent rather than a filler shrub while it fills in.

directions: Curly Locks is a novelty dwarf andromeda whose stems twist and contort as they grow, carrying leaves that curl and spiral rather than lying flat, giving even a young plant a sculptural, almost bonsai-like presence in the winter garden when bare of new growth. Small white spring flowers are secondary to the year-round stem and leaf structure that makes this selection a conversation piece near an entry, in a container, or in a small shaded rock garden. Its slow, dwarf growth habit means little to no pruning is needed beyond removing occasional dead wood. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic and shield the plant from drying winter wind, which can desiccate the twisted, more exposed foliage faster than on flatter-leaved pieris.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade with shelter from cold wind; the wild species is noticeably less cold-hardy than Pieris japonica and its selections.

directions: Pieris formosa is the wild Himalayan and Chinese species behind many garden hybrids and varieties, growing into a much larger, more open large shrub or small tree than the compact japonica cultivars typically sold. Unselected seedlings still show the brilliant coppery-red flush of new spring growth that made the species famous, followed later by drooping panicles of white, urn-shaped flowers. Because it comes from milder mountain forests than Pieris japonica, it needs more reliable warmth and shelter from harsh winter cold and wind to avoid dieback in colder gardens. Give it the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil favored by rhododendrons and camellias, and use it as a large-scale specimen or woodland-edge planting rather than a foundation shrub.

common_name: Rogersii Skimmia (Compact Rounded Male Pollinator Shrub)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade to partial shade, and place within roughly 15-20 feet of female cultivars such as 'Nymans', 'Redruth', or 'Veitchii' to ensure reliable berry set on those plants.

directions: Rogersii is an old, small-scale male Skimmia japonica selection that forms a tight, rounded mound of narrow, dark-green leaves, staying more compact overall than robust male pollinators like 'Fragrans' or 'Rubinetta'. Clusters of reddish-pink buds sit at the branch tips through winter before opening into fragrant, pinkish-white flowers in spring that supply pollen for nearby female plants but never set fruit themselves. Its diminutive scale makes it a good choice for a shaded rock garden, container planting, or tight foundation bed where a full-sized male pollinator would crowd its neighbors. Grow it in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in shade to part shade and prune only lightly right after flowering to preserve its naturally tidy shape.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade to partial shade, and plant within about 15-20 feet of a male cultivar such as 'Rogersii', 'Fragrans', or 'Kew Green' since Foremanii is a female clone and needs a pollen source to fruit heavily.

directions: Foremanii is a long-grown, robust female skimmia valued for its exceptionally heavy crop of bright red berries that persist through winter once a nearby male plant provides pollen. It builds a broader, denser mound than some of the newer compact female selections, with glossy evergreen leaves that show off clusters of ripe fruit particularly well against the dark foliage. Small white spring flowers precede the berries and add mild fragrance to the shaded border, though the fruit display is the main event on this cultivar. Grow it in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to part shade, and avoid pruning after midsummer so as not to remove the wood that carries the coming winter's berry crop.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Cabaret's unusual flower color shows best against a dark evergreen backdrop rather than in a mixed border of yellow-flowered mahonias.

directions: Cabaret is a hybrid mahonia bred from lomariifolia-type parentage and selected for flower spikes in shades of coral and orange rather than the typical bright yellow of most Oregon grape relatives, an unusual color break for the genus. Its bold, spiny, holly-like pinnate leaves and stiff upright canes give the same architectural winter presence as its parent species while the warm-toned flowers open in the cooler months. Deep blue-black berries can follow if a compatible mahonia is flowering nearby, though the plant is grown chiefly for the flower color rather than fruit. Site it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, and remove only dead or overly leggy canes at the base to keep the clump renewing itself.
sources: Great Plant Picks — Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Narihira spreads by suckers into a low colony and works well as a textural groundcover beneath larger shade trees.

directions: Narihira is a selection of the low, spreading Chinese groundcover mahonia distinguished by unusually narrow, almost fern-like leaflets that give it a finer, more delicate texture than the broader-leaved Oregon grape relatives. Short racemes of small yellow flowers appear among the foliage and are followed by dark berries, but the plant is grown primarily for its low, textural groundcover habit beneath taller shade shrubs and trees. It spreads gradually by suckers to knit together a loose colony rather than staying as a single clump, making it useful for covering shaded ground where turf struggles. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, and thin congested canes at the base occasionally to keep the colony open and vigorous.
sources: Great Plant Picks — Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden
